claim: N-glycan branching deficiency triggers the Golgi to generate bioequivalent N-glycans that preserve galectin-glycoprotein interactions and cellular homeostasis.
source: N-glycan branching deficiency triggers the Golgi to generate bioequivalent N-glycans that preserve galectin-glycoprotein interactions and cellular homeostasis.
evidence: This is the main finding stated in the abstract, supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript showing that poly-LacNAc extension compensates for reduced branching.

claim: Galectins bind N-acetyllactosamine (LacNAc) units within N-glycans initiated from UDP-GlcNAc by the medial-Golgi branching enzymes as well as the trans-Golgi poly-LacNAc extension enzyme β1,3-N-acetylglucosaminyltransferase (B3GNT).
source: Galectins bind N-acetyllactosamine (LacNAc) units within N-glycans initiated from UDP-GlcNAc by the medial-Golgi branching enzymes as well as the trans-Golgi poly-LacNAc extension enzyme β1,3-N-acetylglucosaminyltransferase (B3GNT).
evidence: This statement is supported by established knowledge of galectin binding and the experimental design of the study.

claim: Marginally reducing LacNAc content by limiting N-glycans to three branches results in T-cell hyperactivity and autoimmunity.
source: Marginally reducing LacNAc content by limiting N-glycans to three branches results in T-cell hyperactivity and autoimmunity
evidence: This is supported by data from Mgat5 deficient mice showing T-cell hyperactivity and autoimmunity.

claim: Further restricting branching beyond three branches does not produce a more hyperactive state.
source: yet further restricting branching does not produce a more hyperactive state.
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing Mgat2 and Mgat5 deficient T cells, which show similar levels of activation despite different degrees of branching deficiency.

claim: New poly-LacNAc extension by B3GNT maintains galectin binding and immune homeostasis when branching is restricted.
source: Rather, new poly-LacNAc extension by B3GNT maintains galectin binding and immune homeostasis.
evidence: This is supported by data showing increased LEA binding (poly-LacNAc marker) in Mgat2 deficient cells and functional studies with B3gnt2 knockout.

claim: Poly-LacNAc extension is triggered by redistribution of unused UDP-GlcNAc from the medial to trans-Golgi via inter-cisternal tubules.
source: Poly-LacNAc extension is triggered by redistribution of unused UDP-GlcNAc from the medial to trans-Golgi via inter-cisternal tubules.
evidence: This is supported by UDP-GlcNAc measurements in different Golgi compartments and pyrrophenone inhibition experiments.

claim: The galectin-glycoprotein lattice is a dynamic cell surface structure that globally regulates receptor localization and signaling.
source: The galectin-glycoprotein lattice is a dynamic cell surface structure that globally regulates receptor localization and signaling (Demetriou et al., 2001; Partridge et al., 2004; Lau et al., 2007; Dennis et al., 2009; Grigorian et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: The galectin-glycoprotein lattice is involved in basic cellular processes such as signaling, apoptosis, endocytosis, differentiation, and cell growth.
source: Its importance is underscored by its role in basic cellular processes such as signaling, apoptosis, endocytosis, differentiation, and cell growth
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge based on the literature.

claim: The galectin-glycoprotein lattice is associated with a wide range of diseases including immunity/autoimmunity, cancer, and Type 2 diabetes.
source: as well as its association with a wide range of diseases including immunity/autoimmunity (Demetriou et al., 2001; Lee et al., 2007; Mkhikian et al., 2011; Li et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2015; Zhou, 2014), cancer (Dennis et al., 1987; Fernandes et al., 1991; Granovsky et al., 2000; Beheshti Zavareh et al., 2012; Croci et al., 2014), and Type 2 diabetes (Ohtsubo et al., 2005; Johswich et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: The lattice forms due to the multivalent interactions between extracellular galectins and the disaccharide N-acetyllactosamine (LacNAc) present on Asn (N)-linked glycans attached to cell surface glycoproteins.
source: The lattice forms due to the multivalent interactions between extracellular galectins, a family of sugar binding proteins, and the disaccharide N-acetyllactosamine (LacNAc) present on Asn (N)-linked glycans attached to cell surface glycoproteins (Hirabayashi et al., 2002; Brewer et al., 2002; Ahmad et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work establishing the molecular basis of the lattice.

claim: The vast majority of secreted and cell surface proteins are co- or post-translationally modified by the addition of sugars in the ER.
source: The vast majority of secreted and cell surface proteins are co- or post-translationally modified by the addition of sugars in the ER.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of glycobiology.

claim: As proteins transit through the ER and Golgi, their glycans undergo dramatic remodeling, generating a vast and heterogeneous array of glycoforms.
source: As these proteins transit through the ER and Golgi, their glycans undergo dramatic remodeling, generating a vast and heterogeneous array of glycoforms (Kornfeld and Kornfeld, 1985; Schachter, 1991).
evidence: This is supported by citations to foundational work in glycobiology.

claim: In the medial Golgi, MGAT1, 2, 4, and 5 enzymes produce N-glycans with one, two, three, or four N-acetylglucosamine (GlcNAc) branches.
source: In the medial Golgi a group of enzymes, MGAT1, 2, 4, and 5, act to produce N-glycans with one, two, three, or four N-acetylglucosamine (GlcNAc) branches (Schachter, 1986).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work and is established knowledge.

claim: The subsequent addition of galactose by galactosyl transferase enzymes produces the galectin substrate LacNAc.
source: The subsequent addition of galactose by a family of galactosyl transferase enzymes produces the galectin substrate LacNAc (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by reference to a figure showing the pathway and is established knowledge.

claim: The number of branches depends on the relative activity of the medial Golgi branching enzymes MGAT1, 2, 4, and 5 and the availability of their shared donor substrate UDP-GlcNAc.
source: The number of branches depends on the relative activity of the medial Golgi branching enzymes MGAT1, 2, 4, and 5 and the availability of their shared donor substrate UDP-GlcNAc (Lau et al., 2007; Dennis et al., 2009; Grigorian et al., 2007; 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Alternating action of β1,3-N-acetylglucosaminyltransferase (B3GNT) and galactosyl transferase enzymes can generate a linear polymer of LacNAc (poly-LacNAc) at any given branch.
source: Alternating action of β1,3-N-acetylglucosaminyltransferase (B3GNT) and galactosyl transferase enzymes can generate a linear polymer of LacNAc (poly-LacNAc) at any given branch.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the biosynthetic pathway.

claim: Increased LacNAc valency through branching and poly-LacNAc extension can dramatically increase galectin avidity leading to a major impact on cell surface dynamics.
source: Although the affinity of galectin binding to a LacNAc monomer is relatively weak, increased LacNAc valency through branching and poly-LacNAc extension can dramatically increase galectin avidity leading to a major impact on cell surface dynamics (Hirabayashi et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation and represents established understanding of multivalent binding.

claim: In T cells, galectin - T cell receptor (TCR) interactions directly oppose ligand induced TCR clustering and signaling, thereby negatively regulating T cell development, antigen-dependent T cell growth, and autoimmunity risk.
source: In T cells for example, galectin - T cell receptor (TCR) interactions directly oppose ligand induced TCR clustering and signaling, thereby negatively regulating T cell development, antigen-dependent T cell growth, and autoimmunity risk.
evidence: This is based on previous work from the authors' group and represents established findings.

claim: Glycan analysis of tissues from glycosylation pathway deficient mice has revealed the presence of minor but unusual structures.
source: Glycan analysis of tissues from glycosylation pathway deficient mice has revealed the presence of minor but unusual structures (Stone et al., 2009; Takamatsu et al., 2010; Ismail et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Some have suggested that the observed structural alterations may reflect production of bioequivalent glycans that are induced by communication between the cell surface and the Golgi.
source: The function of these changes is unclear, but some have suggested that the observed structural alterations may reflect production of bioequivalent glycans that are induced by communication between the cell surface and the Golgi (Takamatsu et al., 2010; Dam and Brewer, 2010; Dennis and Brewer, 2013).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from previous literature that the current study tests.

claim: Direct evidence supporting the possibility of bioequivalent glycan production is lacking.
source: However, direct evidence supporting this possibility is lacking.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature prior to this study.

claim: Deficiency in MGAT5 reduces avidity for galectin, enhancing antigen dependent and independent TCR clustering/signaling, leading to development of spontaneous autoimmune disease.
source: Deficiency in the branching enzyme β1,6-N-acetylglucosaminyltransferase V (MGAT5) reduces avidity for galectin, enhancing antigen dependent and independent TCR clustering/signaling, leading to development of spontaneous autoimmune disease (Demetriou et al., 2001; Lee et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work from the authors' group.

claim: Based on the current model of the galectin-glycoprotein lattice, more severe reductions in branching should weaken the lattice further and result in greater T cell hyperactivity.
source: Based on the current model of the galectin-glycoprotein lattice, more severe reductions in branching should weaken the lattice further and result in greater T cell hyperactivity.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the existing model that the study tests.

claim: Further limiting branching revealed that the Golgi apparatus has a remarkable capacity to buffer challenges to the strength of the galectin-glycoprotein lattice.
source: Surprisingly, further limiting branching revealed that the Golgi apparatus has a remarkable capacity to buffer challenges to the strength of the galectin-glycoprotein lattice.
evidence: This is a key finding of the study supported by the experimental data.

claim: Loss of Mgat2 is expected to limit N-glycans to a single branch, producing hybrid structures, although a second branch via MGAT4 activity is possible.
source: Loss of Mgat2 is expected to limit N-glycans to a single branch, producing hybrid structures; although a second branch via MGAT4 activity is possible (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on knowledge of the biosynthetic pathway and supported by a figure.

claim: Mgat2 deficiency impacts a much greater percentage of cell surface glycans than Mgat5 deletion.
source: As the branching pathway declines in enzymatic efficiency going from MGAT1 to MGAT5, Mgat2 deficiency also impacts a much greater percentage of cell surface glycans than Mgat5 deletion (Wang et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation and knowledge of enzyme kinetics in the pathway.

claim: Examination of peripheral T cells from Mgat2f/f::Lck-Cre+ mice indicated loss of Mgat2 in most but not all T cells as assayed by flow cytometry with L-PHA.
source: Examination of peripheral T cells from Mgat2f/f::Lck-Cre+ mice indicated loss of Mgat2 in most but not all T cells as assayed by flow cytometry with the plant lectin L-PHA (Phaseolus vulgaris, leukoagglutinin) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: β1,6GlcNAc-branched N-glycans produced by MGAT5 specifically bind L-PHA.
source: β1,6GlcNAc-branched N-glycans produced by MGAT5 specifically bind L-PHA, structures that are also lost following Mgat2 deletion (Demetriou et al., 2001; Cummings and Kornfeld, 1982).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Mgat5 and Mgat2 deficient CD4+ and CD8+ T cells displayed a similar degree of activation and proliferation in response to anti-CD3 despite the more dramatic reduction in LacNAc branching in Mgat2 deficient T cells.
source: Surprisingly, Mgat5 and Mgat2 deficient CD4+ and CD8+ T cells displayed a similar degree of activation and proliferation in response to anti-CD3 (an antibody which induces TCR clustering and signaling) despite the more dramatic reduction in LacNAc branching in Mgat2 deficient T cells (Figure 1A,B,D and E).
evidence: This is a key experimental finding supported by data in the referenced figures.

claim: Mgat5 deletion resulted in a significant reduction in the ability of CD4+ and CD8+ T cells to bind galectin-3.
source: Mgat5 deletion resulted in a significant reduction in the ability of CD4+ and CD8+ T cells to bind galectin-3 (Figure 1C and F), consistent with previously published results (Demetriou et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by data in the referenced figures and citation to previous work.

claim: Mgat2 deficiency produced no additional decrease in galectin-3 binding compared to Mgat5 deficiency.
source: However, Mgat2 deficiency produced no additional decrease in galectin-3 binding (Figure 1C and F), suggesting comparable LacNAc content at the cell surface despite a marked reduction in LacNAc branches in Mgat2 relative to Mgat5 deficient T cells.
evidence: This is a key experimental finding supported by data in the referenced figures.

claim: Compensatory maintenance of cell surface LacNAc content in Mgat2 deficient T cells would primarily occur by poly-LacNAc extension of the MGAT1 generated branch.
source: Since the branching pathway enzymes act sequentially, we hypothesized that compensatory maintenance of cell surface LacNAc content in Mgat2 deficient T cells would primarily occur by poly-LacNAc extension of the MGAT1 generated branch (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on knowledge of the pathway that is then tested experimentally.

claim: LEA binds to poly-LacNAc structures containing at least three repeating LacNAc units.
source: LEA binds to poly-LacNAc structures containing at least three repeating LacNAc units (Kawashima et al., 1990; Merkle and Cummings, 1987).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Wild type and Mgat5-/- T cells and thymocytes expressed very low levels of poly-LacNAc.
source: Wild type and Mgat5-/- T cells and thymocytes expressed very low levels of poly-LacNAc.
evidence: This is supported by LEA staining data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: In Mgat2f/f::Lck-Cre+ mice, loss of L-PHA staining was accompanied by a ~100 fold increase in LEA staining.
source: However, in Mgat2f/f::Lck-Cre+ mice, loss of L-PHA staining was accompanied by a ~100 fold increase in LEA staining.
evidence: This is a key experimental finding supported by data in Figure 1G.

claim: The loss of L-PHA binding and the increase in LEA binding appeared to occur concurrently during the double positive stage of thymocyte development, shortly after the Lck promoter driven Cre is first expressed, and were maintained through the single positive stage and in peripheral T cells.
source: The loss of L-PHA binding and the increase in LEA binding appeared to occur concurrently during the double positive stage of thymocyte development, shortly after the Lck promoter driven Cre is first expressed, and were maintained through the single positive stage and in peripheral T cells (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by developmental analysis shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Treatment of various cell types with swainsonine indicated that homeostatic up-regulation of poly-LacNAc was a general feature of many cell types including epithelial, mesenchymal, and hematopoietic cells; with the greatest responses in the latter.
source: Treatment of various cell types with swainsonine (SW), a mannosidase II inhibitor which blocks N-glycan processing between MGAT1 and MGAT2 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), indicated that homeostatic up-regulation of poly-LacNAc was a general feature of many cell types including epithelial, mesenchymal, and hematopoietic cells; with the greatest responses in the latter (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1H showing LEA induction across multiple cell types.

claim: Poly-LacNAc may occur on N-glycans as well as O-glycans and glycolipids.
source: Poly-LacNAc may occur on N-glycans as well as O-glycans and glycolipids (Fukuda et al., 1986; Watanabe et al., 1979).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: LEA has been reported to bind to high-mannose structures in addition to poly-LacNAc.
source: Furthermore, LEA has been reported to bind to high-mannose structures in addition to poly-LacNAc (Oguri, 2005).
evidence: This is based on a citation to previous work.

claim: PNGase F treatment of live cells incompletely removes N-glycans, with a four hour treatment of Mgat2f/f T cells reducing cell surface L-PHA binding by ~50%.
source: PNGase F treatment of live cells incompletely removes N-glycans, with a four hour treatment of Mgat2f/f T cells reducing cell surface L-PHA binding by ~50% (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in the referenced figure supplement.

claim: PNGase F treatment resulted in a >80% reduction in LEA binding in Mgat2 deficient T cells, suggesting that the vast majority of LEA staining was due to cell surface N-glycans.
source: Nevertheless, the same treatment resulted in a >80% reduction in LEA binding in Mgat2 deficient T cells, suggesting that the vast majority of LEA staining was due to cell surface N-glycans (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in the referenced figure supplement.

claim: Mgat1 deficiency blocks all branching and poly-LacNAc extension in N-glycans, but not O-glycans or glycolipids.
source: Mgat1 deficiency blocks all branching and poly-LacNAc extension in N-glycans, but not O-glycans or glycolipids.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of the biosynthetic pathway.

claim: Unlike Mgat2 deficiency, Mgat1 deficient thymocytes do not show an increase in LEA staining concurrent with the loss in L-PHA staining.
source: Indeed, unlike Mgat2 deficiency, Mgat1 deficient thymocytes do not show an increase in LEA staining concurrent with the loss in L-PHA staining (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a key experimental finding supported by data in Figure 2A.

claim: SW increases LEA staining in CHO cells but not Mgat1 deficient CHO (Lec1) cells.
source: Similarly, SW increases LEA staining in CHO cells but not Mgat1 deficient CHO (Lec1) cells (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figures 2B and C.

claim: Increased LEA staining induced by SW treatment of T cells was reversed by the mannosidase I inhibitors deoxymannojirimycin (DMN) and kifunensine (kif), which block the N-glycan pathway prior to MGAT1.
source: Furthermore, increased LEA staining induced by SW treatment of T cells was reversed by the mannosidase I inhibitors deoxymannojirimycin (DMN) and kifunensine (kif), which block the N-glycan pathway prior to MGAT1 (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 2D.

claim: MALDI-TOF-MS of N-glycans derived from SW treated Jurkat T cells confirmed the presence of hybrid N-glycans with up to two poly-LacNAc extended branches.
source: MALDI-TOF-MS of N-glycans derived from SW treated Jurkat T cells confirmed the presence of hybrid N-glycans with up to two poly-LacNAc extended branches (m/z 2897, 3102, 3347, 3551, and 4000 in Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data in the referenced figures.

claim: Endo-β-galactosidase digestion confirmed the presence of longer poly-LacNAc chains after SW treatment.
source: The non-treated cells had a ratio of 0.5, which increased to 1.1 in the SW treated cells (Figure 2F and G), confirming the presence of longer poly-LacNAc chains after SW treatment.
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data after enzymatic digestion shown in Figures 2F and G.

claim: SW treatment alone moderately reduced galectin-3 binding, but the addition of kifunensine dramatically reduced galectin-3 binding of Jurkat T cells.
source: Whereas SW treatment alone moderately reduced galectin-3 binding, the addition of kifunensine dramatically reduced galectin-3 binding of Jurkat T cells (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 3A.

claim: SW treatment alone caused significant increases in both anti-CD3 induced activation and proliferation of primary human T cells.
source: As previously shown, SW treatment alone caused significant increases in both anti-CD3 induced activation and proliferation of primary human T cells (Figure 3B,C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in the referenced figures.

claim: The addition of kifunensine or DMN to SW treatment resulted in much greater T cell hyperactivity, particularly at lower doses of anti-CD3.
source: However, the addition of kifunensine or DMN resulted in much greater hyperactivity, particularly at lower doses of anti-CD3.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figures 3B and C.

claim: Careful titration of kifunensine in the presence of SW caused a dose dependent decrease in LEA binding and increase in CD69 induction, indicating that poly-LacNAc extension dose dependently regulates T cell activation thresholds.
source: Careful titration of kifunensine in the presence of SW did not further reduce L-PHA binding, yet caused a dose dependent decrease in LEA binding and increase in CD69 induction, indicating that poly-LacNAc extension dose dependently regulates T cell activation thresholds (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is supported by dose-response data in the referenced figure supplement.

claim: T cells from Mgat2f/f::Lck-Cre+::B3gnt2-/- mice showed significantly reduced galectin-3 binding when compared to Mgat2 deficient T cells, confirming reduced LacNAc content.
source: Indeed, T cells from Mgat2f/f::Lck-Cre+::B3gnt2-/- mice showed significantly reduced galectin-3 binding when compared to Mgat2 deficient T cells, confirming reduced LacNAc content (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 3D.

claim: Both genetic and pharmacological inhibition of homeostatic poly-LacNAc extension resulted in significantly increased T cell hyperactivity.
source: Directly comparing T cell activation between these lines showed that both genetic and pharmacological inhibition of homeostatic poly-LacNAc extension resulted in significantly increased T cell hyperactivity (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 3E.

claim: Vehicle treated Mgat2f/f::Lck-Cre+ mice displayed a significantly more severe EAE than vehicle treated Mgat2f/f mice.
source: As expected, vehicle treated Mgat2f/f::Lck-Cre+ mice displayed a significantly more severe EAE than vehicle treated Mgat2f/f mice.
evidence: This is supported by EAE clinical score data in Figure 3F.

claim: Kifunensine treatment of Mgat2f/f::Lck-Cre+ mice resulted in a dramatic increase in clinical score and disease incidence early in the disease course.
source: However, kifunensine treatment of Mgat2f/f::Lck-Cre+ mice resulted in a dramatic increase in clinical score and disease incidence early in the disease course, a difference that narrowed later in the absence of kifunensine (Figure 3F and Figure 3—supplement figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by EAE data in the referenced figures.

claim: Kifunensine treated mice had more pro-inflammatory TH1 and TH17 cells compared to vehicle treated mice in vivo and following re-stimulation with MOG 35–55 in vitro.
source: Kifunensine treated mice also had more pro-inflammatory TH1 and TH17 cells compared to vehicle treated mice in vivo and following re-stimulation with MOG 35–55 in vitro (Figure 3G, Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by cytokine analysis data in the referenced figures.

claim: The increase in LEA binding began within ~1.5 hr of SW treatment, indicating an almost immediate compensatory response.
source: Although the increase in LEA binding trailed slightly behind an increase in ConA binding, it began to increase within ~1.5 hr of SW treatment, indicating an almost immediate compensatory response.
evidence: This is supported by time course data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Blocking TCR signaling genetically or pharmacologically only partially reduced the magnitude of the poly-LacNAc response induced by SW.
source: Blocking TCR signaling genetically, with TCRβ and Lck deficient Jurkat lines, or pharmacologically, with MAP kinase inhibitors, only partially reduced the magnitude of the poly-LacNAc response induced by SW (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in the referenced figures.

claim: Directly activating downstream TCR signaling with PMA and ionomycin did not induce poly-LacNAc up-regulation, although it further enhanced poly-LacNAc triggered by SW.
source: More importantly, directly activating downstream TCR signaling with PMA and ionomycin did not induce poly-LacNAc up-regulation, although it further enhanced poly-LacNAc triggered by SW (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 4B.

claim: TCR signaling appears to be neither necessary nor sufficient for the homeostatic poly-LacNAc response, but does contribute to its magnitude in the context of deficient branching.
source: Thus, TCR signaling appears to be neither necessary nor sufficient for the homeostatic poly-LacNAc response, but does contribute to its magnitude in the context of deficient branching.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data with TCR signaling manipulations.

claim: Microarray analysis of purified Mgat2+/+ and Mgat2-/- CD4+ T cells revealed no significant changes in glycosylation genes known to impact poly-LacNAc production or UDP-GlcNAc biosynthesis.
source: Microarray analysis of purified Mgat2+/+ and Mgat2-/- CD4+ T cells revealed no significant changes in glycosylation genes known to impact poly-LacNAc production or UDP-GlcNAc biosynthesis (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by microarray data presented in Table 1.

claim: Comparing B3GNT2 protein levels in Jurkat T cells treated with or without SW showed no difference.
source: Comparing B3GNT2 protein levels in Jurkat T cells treated with or without SW also showed no difference (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 4C.

claim: Total poly-LacNAc enzyme activity in lysates from control and SW treated Jurkat T cells revealed no difference.
source: Total poly-LacNAc enzyme activity in lysates from control and SW treated Jurkat T cells also revealed no difference (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by enzyme activity assay data in Figure 4D.

claim: Increased B3GNT enzyme activity is not responsible for the homeostatic up-regulation of poly-LacNAc induced by branching deficiency.
source: Thus, increased B3GNT enzyme activity is not responsible for the homeostatic up-regulation of poly-LacNAc induced by branching deficiency.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the enzyme activity and protein level data.

claim: All three UDP-GlcNAc transporters localized to the cis and medial Golgi compartments while B3GNT2 localized to a later Golgi compartment.
source: All three UDP-GlcNAc transporters localized to the cis and medial Golgi compartments while B3GNT2 localized to a later Golgi compartment (Figure 5A–E).
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy and line scan analysis data in Figures 5A-E.

claim: Overexpression of the UDP-GlcNAc transporters did not drive poly-LacNAc production.
source: In addition, overexpression of the UDP-GlcNAc transporters did not drive poly-LacNAc production (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 5F.

claim: The trans Golgi is comparatively deficient in UDP-GlcNAc, thereby limiting B3GNT activity and poly-LacNAc extension under steady state conditions.
source: These results suggest that the trans Golgi is comparatively deficient in UDP-GlcNAc, thereby limiting B3GNT activity and poly-LacNAc extension under steady state conditions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the localization data and overexpression experiments.

claim: SW treatment did not alter the Golgi localization of the three UDP-GlcNAc transporters or B3GNT2.
source: However, SW treatment did not alter the Golgi localization of the three UDP-GlcNAc transporters or B3GNT2, arguing against this possibility (Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: This is supported by localization data comparing control and SW treated cells in the referenced figures.

claim: Measuring UDP-GlcNAc by LC-MS/MS in a whole cell vesicular fraction isolated from post nuclear supernatant revealed significant levels of UDP-GlcNAc.
source: Measuring UDP-GlcNAc by LC-MS/MS in a whole cell vesicular fraction isolated from post nuclear supernatant revealed significant levels of UDP-GlcNAc (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data in the referenced figure supplement.

claim: Treatment of post nuclear supernatant with 0.1% Triton-X or 50 mM UMP significantly reduced the amount of UDP-GlcNAc in the vesicular fraction, confirming UDP-GlcNAc was located in vesicles containing UDP-GlcNAc/UMP anti-porters.
source: Both treatments significantly reduced the amount of UDP-GlcNAc in the vesicular fraction, confirming UDP-GlcNAc was located in vesicles containing UDP-GlcNAc/UMP anti-porters (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in the referenced figure supplement.

claim: UDP-GlcNAc levels were elevated in the vesicular but not the cytosolic fractions of kifunensine treated Jurkat T cells.
source: Consistent with our hypothesis, UDP-GlcNAc levels were elevated in the vesicular but not the cytosolic fractions of kifunensine treated Jurkat T cells (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data in Figure 6A.

claim: UDP-GlcNAc was elevated in the Golgi of kifunensine treated Jurkat T cells despite no difference in total cellular or cytosolic UDP-GlcNAc levels.
source: UDP-GlcNAc was elevated in the Golgi of kifunensine treated Jurkat T cells despite no difference in total cellular or cytosolic UDP-GlcNAc levels (Figures 4G,6A,C).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data in the referenced figures.

claim: TGN46 immuno-isolated vesicles from Brefeldin A treated Jurkat T cells were partially depleted for cis and medial Golgi markers relative to trans Golgi markers including B3GNT2, confirming relative enrichment of the trans/TGN compartment.
source: TGN46 immuno-isolated vesicles from Brefeldin A treated Jurkat T cells were partially depleted for cis and medial Golgi markers relative to trans Golgi markers including B3GNT2, confirming relative enrichment of the trans/TGN compartment (Figure 6D and E).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figures 6D and E.

claim: Vesicles from kifunensine treated Jurkat T cells demonstrated increased UDP-GlcNAc relative to control, indicating that UDP-GlcNAc levels rise in the trans Golgi when medial Golgi branching activity is significantly diminished.
source: Vesicles from kifunensine treated Jurkat T cells demonstrated increased UDP-GlcNAc relative to control (Figure 6F), indicating that UDP-GlcNAc levels rise in the trans Golgi when medial Golgi branching activity is significantly diminished.
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data in Figure 6F.

claim: Nocodazole, which interrupts longitudinal but not vertical Golgi tubules, had no effect on poly-LacNAc induction by SW in Jurkat T cells.
source: Nocodazole, which interrupts longitudinal but not vertical Golgi tubules, had no effect on poly-LacNAc induction by SW in Jurkat T cells (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 6G.

claim: Pyrrophenone significantly blocked SW induced up-regulation of poly-LacNAc in Jurkat T cells in a dose dependent manner.
source: In contrast, pyrrophenone disrupts both longitudinal and inter-cisternal vertical tubules via inhibition of cytosolic phospholipase A2-α (San Pietro et al., 2009). Pyrrophenone significantly blocked SW induced up-regulation of poly-LacNAc in Jurkat T cells in a dose dependent manner, as indicated by comparing its effects on LEA and ConA staining; the latter controlling for any changes in Golgi transport (Figure 6H and Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by dose-response data in the referenced figures.

claim: Pyrrophenone had no effect on ConA, LEA, or L-PHA levels in control Jurkat T cells lacking SW.
source: In contrast, pyrrophenone had no effect on ConA, LEA, or L-PHA levels in control Jurkat T cells lacking SW (Figure 6—supplement figure 1F–H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in the referenced figure supplement.

claim: When branching enzymes under-utilize UDP-GlcNAc in the medial Golgi, UDP-GlcNAc accumulates and then shifts by diffusion to the trans Golgi via inter-cisternal tubules, thereby increasing substrate supply to B3GNT and triggering poly-LacNAc extension.
source: We conclude that when branching enzymes under-utilize UDP-GlcNAc in the medial Golgi, UDP-GlcNAc accumulates and then shifts by diffusion to the trans Golgi via inter-cisternal tubules, thereby increasing substrate supply to B3GNT and triggering poly-LacNAc extension (Figure 7).
evidence: This is the main mechanistic conclusion of the study, supported by the UDP-GlcNAc measurements and pyrrophenone inhibition data.

claim: Structurally disparate glycans are functionally equivalent based on LacNAc content.
source: Our data demonstrates that structurally disparate glycans are functionally equivalent based on LacNAc content and suggests a novel self-correcting mechanism in the Golgi that sustains cellular homeostasis by ensuring LacNAc content is maintained at a minimal level within N-glycans.
evidence: This is a key conclusion of the study based on the functional equivalence of Mgat2 and Mgat5 deficient T cells.

claim: The Golgi has a novel self-correcting mechanism that sustains cellular homeostasis by ensuring LacNAc content is maintained at a minimal level within N-glycans.
source: Our data demonstrates that structurally disparate glycans are functionally equivalent based on LacNAc content and suggests a novel self-correcting mechanism in the Golgi that sustains cellular homeostasis by ensuring LacNAc content is maintained at a minimal level within N-glycans.
evidence: This is the main conceptual conclusion of the study.

claim: The similar degree of hyperactivity between Mgat5 and Mgat2 deficient T cells indicates that poly-LacNAc extended hybrid structures are functionally equivalent to complex tri-antennary structures.
source: The similar degree of hyperactivity between Mgat5 and Mgat2 deficient T cells indicates that poly-LacNAc extended hybrid structures are functionally equivalent to complex tri-antennary structures.
evidence: This is an inference based on the functional data comparing the two genotypes.

claim: Blockade of mannosidase II and Mgat2 deficiency produced a similar phenotype, which was blocked/reversed by both mannosidase I inhibition and Mgat1 deficiency, despite each targeting distinct biochemical steps and resulting in distinct structures.
source: Importantly, blockade of mannosidase II and Mgat2 deficiency produced a similar phenotype, which was blocked/reversed by both mannosidase I inhibition and Mgat1 deficiency, despite each targeting distinct biochemical steps and resulting in distinct structures.
evidence: This is based on the experimental data with different inhibitors and genetic models.

claim: Structurally diverse glycans are biologically equivalent if they share a similar amount of LacNAc.
source: Thus, our data demonstrate that structurally diverse glycans are biologically equivalent if they share a similar amount of LacNAc.
evidence: This is a key conclusion based on the functional equivalence data.

claim: The overall glycan structure sets the total LacNAc content, thereby largely determining avidity of binding for galectins.
source: The overall glycan structure sets the total LacNAc content, thereby largely determining avidity of binding for galectins.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data and understanding of multivalent binding.

claim: Glycan diversity may be collapsed into a much smaller group of bioequivalent structures based on the number of structural subunits within the overall glycan that bind to a given animal lectin.
source: Our data suggests that glycan diversity may be collapsed into a much smaller group of bioequivalent structures based on the number of structural subunits within the overall glycan that bind to a given animal lectin.
evidence: This is a conceptual inference based on the findings of functional equivalence.

claim: N-glycosylation is an essential biosynthetic pathway necessary for cellular homeostasis and mammalian development.
source: N-glycosylation is an essential biosynthetic pathway necessary for cellular homeostasis and mammalian development (Dennis et al., 2009), yet lacks a known self-correcting mechanism.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Homeostatic control of LacNAc content does not result from changes in enzyme levels/activity or metabolic production of UDP-GlcNAc substrate.
source: Our data suggest that homeostatic control of LacNAc content does not result from changes in enzyme levels/activity or metabolic production of UDP-GlcNAc substrate; but rather appears to arise from the structure of the Golgi.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the microarray, Western blot, enzyme activity, and UDP-GlcNAc measurement data.

claim: The UDP-GlcNAc transporters preferentially supply UDP-GlcNAc to the cis/medial over trans Golgi, thus prioritizing branching over extension.
source: Our data indicate that the UDP-GlcNAc transporters preferentially supply UDP-GlcNAc to the cis/medial over trans Golgi, thus prioritizing branching over extension.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the localization data and functional studies.

claim: The segmented organization of enzymes and transporters allows for local depletion of substrate prior to diffusion to other compartments.
source: Despite the presence of continuities between Golgi cisterna and previous work arguing that the Golgi is functionally interconnected (Kim et al., 2001), our data suggest that the segmented organization of enzymes and transporters allows for local depletion of substrate prior to diffusion to other compartments.
evidence: This is an inference based on the localization and UDP-GlcNAc distribution data.

claim: The evolutionary placement of the B3GNT poly-LacNAc extension enzymes in the trans Golgi provides a backup mechanism that captures unused UDP-GlcNAc from the medial Golgi shunted via inter-cisternal tubules.
source: In this manner, the evolutionary placement of the B3GNT poly-LacNAc extension enzymes in the trans Golgi provides a backup mechanism that captures unused UDP-GlcNAc from the medial Golgi shunted via inter-cisternal tubules.
evidence: This is a conceptual inference about the evolutionary significance of the findings.

claim: This backup system may explain the lack of evolutionary pressure to produce genetic redundancy in the Golgi branching enzymes in mammals.
source: This backup system may also explain the lack of evolutionary pressure to produce genetic redundancy in the Golgi branching enzymes in mammals and the dramatically more severe phenotype seen with Mgat1 deficiency, which blocks all production of N-glycan LacNAc, compared to other Mgat genes (Ioffe and Stanley, 1994; Metzler et al., 1994).
evidence: This is a speculative inference about evolutionary implications.

claim: High protein transit rates present a significant challenge to the Golgi and have the potential to reduce the medial Golgi branching efficiency by decreasing the time available for branching reactions.
source: High protein transit rates present a significant challenge to the Golgi and have the potential to reduce the medial Golgi branching efficiency by decreasing the time available for branching reactions.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential physiological challenges.

claim: Having a back-up system that provides poly-LacNAc extension in the trans Golgi by capturing unused UDP-GlcNAc from the medial Golgi would be critical for the maintenance of the lattice at a minimal essential level.
source: Under this scenario, having a back-up system that provides poly-LacNAc extension in the trans Golgi by capturing unused UDP-GlcNAc from the medial Golgi would be critical for the maintenance of the lattice at a minimal essential level.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the functional significance of the mechanism.

claim: A second step in the assembly line would act to counteract the moment to moment variability and stochastic uncertainty of glycan synthesis.
source: Even in an unstressed system, a second step in the assembly line would act to counteract the moment to moment variability and stochastic uncertainty of glycan synthesis.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the general function of the mechanism.

claim: The effectiveness of SW as an anti-cancer therapeutic is likely limited by compensatory poly-LacNAc production.
source: For example, the effectiveness of SW as an anti-cancer therapeutic is likely limited by compensatory poly-LacNAc production (Goss et al., 1994; 1997).
evidence: This is a speculative inference about therapeutic implications based on the findings.

claim: Therapeutic strategies aimed at disrupting the lattice should block branching and extension simultaneously, or target a more proximal regulator such as UDP-GlcNAc metabolism or transport.
source: Thus, therapeutic strategies aimed at disrupting the lattice should block branching and extension simultaneously, or target a more proximal regulator such as UDP-GlcNAc metabolism or transport.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the findings of the study.

claim: Increased availability and use of UDP-GlcNAc in the trans Golgi would increase uridine-monophosphate (UMP) levels, thereby driving anti-port of UDP-Galactose into the trans Golgi to promote further extension with poly-LacNAc rather than capping by sialic acid.
source: Increased availability and use of UDP-GlcNAc in the trans Golgi would increase uridine-monophosphate (UMP) levels, thereby driving anti-port of UDP-Galactose into the trans Golgi to promote further extension with poly-LacNAc rather than capping by sialic acid.
evidence: This is a mechanistic inference about how the antiport system coordinates extension.

claim: Were sialic acid also charged with UDP rather than cytidine-monophosphate (CMP), UDP-GlcNAc usage in the trans Golgi would drive import of UDP-Sialic acid and capping equally with UDP-Galactose and extension.
source: Were sialic acid also charged with UDP rather than cytidine-monophosphate (CMP), UDP-GlcNAc usage in the trans Golgi would drive import of UDP-Sialic acid and capping equally with UDP-Galactose and extension.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about why different nucleotides are used for different sugars.

claim: B3GNT2 is one of the major B3GNT enzymes responsible for poly-LacNAc branch extension in mouse T cells.
source: B3GNT2 is one of the major B3GNT enzymes responsible for poly-LacNAc branch extension in mouse T cells and poly-LacNAc up-regulation is expected to be limited in its absence (Togayachi et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.
